milestones.title: Pueblo de Los Ángeles founded
milestones.detail: On 4 September 1781 a group of 44 settlers founds the pueblo under Spanish governor Felipe de Neve, beside the Tongva village of Yaanga.

milestones.title: Flood moves the plaza to higher ground
milestones.detail: A great flood in 1815 shifts the Los Angeles River's channel; the plaza church, begun in 1814, is moved to higher ground at its present site.

milestones.title: Under Mexican rule
milestones.detail: After the Mexican War of Independence the pueblo becomes part of Mexico in 1821; it is still a small ranch town of about 650 people.

milestones.title: Taken by the United States
milestones.detail: US forces first raise their flag over the town in August 1846; fighting with the Californios ends with the Treaty of Cahuenga on 13 January 1847, and California is ceded in 1848.

milestones.title: Incorporated as an American city
milestones.detail: Los Angeles is incorporated as a municipality on 4 April 1850, five months before California becomes a state. The first census counts 1,610 residents.

milestones.title: Southern Pacific railroad arrives
milestones.detail: The Southern Pacific line from San Francisco to Los Angeles is completed in 1876.

milestones.title: Santa Fe railroad and the land boom
milestones.detail: The Santa Fe line from Chicago is completed in 1885 and migrants flood in; the population grows from 11,183 in 1880 to 50,395 in 1890.

milestones.title: Hollywood merges into Los Angeles
milestones.detail: Hollywood joins the city in 1910, when ten film companies already operate in Los Angeles; by 1921 more than 80 percent of the world's film industry is concentrated there.

milestones.title: Los Angeles Aqueduct opens
milestones.detail: The aqueduct, built under William Mulholland, begins delivering water from the Owens River in November 1913 and allows the city to keep expanding.

milestones.title: San Fernando Valley annexed
milestones.detail: By referendum, 170 square miles of the San Fernando Valley and the Palms district are added to the city, almost tripling its area.

milestones.title: Summer Olympic Games
milestones.detail: Los Angeles hosts the Summer Olympics for the first time.

milestones.title: Arroyo Seco Parkway opens
milestones.detail: The parkway to Pasadena, one of the oldest freeways in the United States, mostly opens in 1940.

milestones.title: Watts riots
milestones.detail: Racial tensions lead to the Watts riots in 1965, which leave 34 people dead and over 1,000 injured.

milestones.title: Second Olympic Games
milestones.detail: Los Angeles hosts the Summer Olympics for the second time.

milestones.title: Metro Rail opens
milestones.detail: The first line of the modern Metro Rail system (today's A Line) opens in 1990.

milestones.title: Northridge earthquake
milestones.detail: A magnitude 6.7 earthquake shakes the city in 1994, causing $12.5 billion in damage and 72 deaths.

milestones.title: Palisades Fire
milestones.detail: In January 2025 wind-driven wildfires sweep Southern California; the Palisades Fire causes widespread destruction in the Pacific Palisades district.

landmarks.name: Continental Building
landmarks.note: 175 ft; the city's first skyscraper and its tallest building until 1928.

landmarks.name: Hollywood Sign
landmarks.note: Erected in 1923 as 'HOLLYWOODLAND' in letters 50 ft (15.2 m) tall; rebuilt in 1978 with letters 44 ft (13.4 m) tall.

landmarks.source: Whiteson, Leon (1989), The Watts Towers of Los Angeles, Mosaic Press, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts_Towers

notes: Start date is not contested: the pueblo was founded on 4 September 1781 (the Tongva village of Yaanga already stood on the site). The plaza moved to its present position after the 1815 flood, so the historic core point is the present Plaza. Population before 1850 is thin: no regular counts were taken, and only five points could be sourced (1781, about 1790, about 1820, and the censuses of 1836 and 1844). The 1836 and 1844 values add the separately reported 'gente de razon' and Indian counts. Wikipedia also gives 1,680 for 1841; it is not used because its coverage is unclear. The 1850 federal census (1,610) was taken in early 1851 by one enumerator and is lower than the 1844 count. Figures from 1850 to 1940 are US census counts for the city of Los Angeles within its boundaries at the time, which grew hugely by annexation (for example the San Fernando Valley in 1915); they are city-proper counts, while the UN series from 1950 covers the wider urban agglomeration, so expect a step up at 1950 (Chandler's agglomeration estimates: 107,000 in 1900, 480,000 in 1914, 1,147,000 in 1925). Landmarks: tower heights and completion years are from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center, whose completion years for the Aon Center (1974) and U.S. Bank Tower (1990) are a year later than the dates often quoted. Los Angeles has few tall pre-1900 monuments and none with a sourced height: the Avila Adobe (1818), the Plaza Church (1822), the Pico House and the Bradbury Building (1893) are left out for that reason, as are Griffith Observatory, the Memorial Coliseum, Union Station, the Theme Building at LAX, Dodger Stadium and Walt Disney Concert Hall.
